subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority, introduced by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), and to speak against the most recent amendment. This Bill means the Government is seeking authority to borrow $23.3 billion. Of that amount, $7.3 billion is for the fiscal year 1984-85, and the balance of $16 billion is for the next fiscal year, 1985-86. Of the $7.3 billion, I think it is noteworthy that $5.3 billion reflects further financial requirements resulting from the deficit inherited from the former government. The remaining $2 billion may be carried over into the fiscal year 1985-86. Of the $16 billion being borrowed for the next fiscal year, none may be carried over to the following fiscal year.
The $2 billion reserve I spoke of for this year is designed to provide flexibility in the event of large, unpredictable changes in the Government's financial requirements; for example, the foreign exchange operations to stabilize the dollar may be required. The $16 billion is expected to meet borrowing demands until next fall, and legislation will probably be introduced following the Budget next spring to cover the remaining part of the fiscal year.
As Shakespeare put it in Hamlet, Mr. Speaker: "Neither a borrower not a lender be". I think most Canadians will acknowledge the wisdom of that statement. No one wants to borrow money for the operation of a household or business or, in this case, government. But as desirable and agreeable as that statement is, I think Canadians will acknowledge just how necessary this borrowing is. The previous government left a legacy of crippling debt for Canadians and thus necessitated this borrowing Bill.
The saddest part of all this, Mr. Speaker, is that there should be no deficit. If we look at the past decade from the years 1969 to 1979, there were times of record economic growth. As some provinces have demonstrated, we have seen that by proper financial management and fiscal housekeeping a government should emerge from good economic times and a strong vibrant economy with a surplus. But this was not the case here. As one of the outgoing Ministers quite rightly put it, we have a bare cupboard. Because of this background of wasteful spending we find ourselves having to approach this House seeking authority to borrow more money.
Over the course of this debate it has been interesting to listen to the use of the word "hypocrisy". The critics have said that this debate involves hypocrisy because of this Party's opposition to borrowing Bills when it was the Official Opposition and the now Opposition's position against borrowing Bills, given the fact they were the government that incurred all of this debt. This allegation of hypocrisy comes from the third Party in this House, the Party that believes the economy will get going again if the Government puts dollars directly into the
December 4, 1984

pockets of the people. On the face of it that might sound good until one begins to examine the economic foolishness inherent in that statement. Someone has to pay for government handouts, which means taxation and deficit financing, which is what got us into the situation we are in.
This allegation of hypocrisy is interesting also because it is only half right. As we examine the statement of the financial cupboard, Mr. Speaker, we can see that this Government is left with no alternatives. However, the Official Opposition, when it was in government, did have alternatives over the decade of prosperity. It could have bequeathed to Canadians a much stronger and vibrant economy than it did. If one is to talk about hypocrisy, then indeed that is the boldest form of it.
If we look to this morning's edition of the national newspaper we can see the kind of spending that resulted in this deficit. We see the squandering by the former Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). His government brought us to the point where one dollar in every three is needed just to service the debt. His government was spending $264 million every day or, to bring it down to something more understandable, $190,000 a minute. His government held this absolutely perverse rationale that by giving people money from the government, that would somehow solve the long-term economic problems. We have found instead a record deficit, record high interest rates and record pressures on the Canadian people. This is what we have been left, but there is hope.
I think all of us would agree, Mr. Speaker, with the hope we found in the statement by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the hope as exemplified in what he talked about as the four positions we must take as the Government. First, we must put our own fiscal house in order and get control of government spending. Second, we must redefine the role of government as a player in the economy. Third, we must adopt policies that foster investment. Fourth, we must bring about changes in a fair, open and equitable manner.
The expenditure cuts and other measures announced by the Minister of Finance will hold next year's deficit at $34.9 billion, a level only marginally larger than this year and considerably lower than the $37 billion projected by the previous government. Canadians have seen others suffer the tragic consequences of a government that spends so much more money than it brings in, the negative economic ripple effect which has resulted in high interest rates and a lack of investor and consumer confidence. The message should be abundantly clear to all Members of this House: responsible deficit management is needed. We do not need what the third Party of this country has advocated-reckless spending.
It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that we have come before this House seeking passage of Bill C-ll. It is for these reasons that we are left with no other choice. Therefore, I support Bill C-ll, I agree with the necessity to borrow, and I thank you for the opportunity to address this issue before the House.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had a chance to listen to our new colleague from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake and I welcome him to this House. I was very interested to hear him talking so much about the deficit, about Shakespeare and all those fine words. He also talked about our Party and the deficits we would like to run.
I would like to ask him about a very real situation back home. Under the Douglas Government of the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s, the Government of Woodrow Lloyd, and on through that of Allan Blakeney, we did not have deficits in our province. In fact, two years ago when the Blakeney Government was defeated, there was no deficit in the Province of Saskatchewan. Now all of a sudden, after two years of Tory rule, there is a deficit of over $800 million in the Province of Saskatchewan. In a province of only one million people, that is a deficit of over $800 for every single man, woman and child.
Why would the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake accuse us of being a Party which likes to run up huge debts when the record speaks so clearly? When one compares the NDP record in Saskatchewan against that of his party, it is clear that the Party of irresponsibility and deficit financing is the Party of the Hon. Member. In fact, according to the statistics I have here, the number of people on welfare in Saskatchewan has gone up in the last two and one-half years by 73 per cent. How can the Member stand in his place and say that our Party is the Party that likes to drive up government debts when indeed the record speaks clearly for itself?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) for asking that question. It is an honour for me to respond to his comments. It is an opportunity I have long waited for.
Two years ago, after the prosperous decade of growth which I spoke of earlier, the Province of Alberta had untold billions of dollars. The Province of Saskatchewan came in with a balanced budget every time. A lot of us thought that was odd because if the government was indeed playing in the fair market in the real world there should be a surplus. Then we looked at the books and found that through third party lending on Crown corporations and very creative bookkeeping the state-oriented type of government which this Party advocates and has been so fond of would have bankrupted Saskatchewan. However, the interesting type of bookkeeping which we saw resulted simply in a balanced budget.
With all due respect and honour to be accorded to the new government, they have simply opened the books of the Government of Saskatchewan to look at how the New Democratic Party would run a government. What we found has resulted in an $800 million deficit. This is a warning to the people of Saskatchewan for the 1986 election and a warning to the people of Canada about what would ever happen in the country if that kind of Party even became the Official Opposition rather than simply the third party rump of Canadian politics.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I stand today in support of Bill C-l 1, an Act to provide borrowing authority, presented by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), I must say that I deplore the circumstances that have led us to this point. There is not one of us in this Conservative Government who would willingly lend himself or herself to the prospect of increasing the national debt and the burden on the Canadian taxpayer. We are just beginning to realize the depth of the financial hole in which we have been left by previous governments. The job of climbing back out of that hole has only just begun.
The Minister of State for Finance has asked that our borrowing power be increased by $7.3 billion for this fiscal year. That will take care of current commitments and allow for a $2 billion contingency fund that, if not needed, will be carried over into the next fiscal year. This reserve fund will allow flexibility in the event of unpredictable fluctuations in our financial requirements, such as changes in the exchange rates and the value of our Canadian dollar. Looking forward into the next year, the Minister has asked for authority to borrow $16 billion more for fiscal 1985-86.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this estimate of our spending needs is a sound one and the request for borrowing is born of necessity. While we are apparently still on the same Keynesian track that led us into this morass, we are not, as a Government, committed to handing out money pell-mell, as was the last administration. The course we set with the passing of this Bill, coupled with the measures set forth in the Finance Minister's economic statement, will lead us out of our debt-ridden circumstances and on to the road to fiscal recovery.
Let us look at why we are now in this state today. Let us look at what led us here. We have inherited a situation with this Government that I believe to be unique in Canadian history. We are following a dynasty of Liberalism that led this country down the garden path. In talking of economic mismanagement, I shall quote from a book entitled Business Cycles in Canada by Maurice Lamontagne, excerpts from which are found on pages 73-82 in the 1984 paper of the Canadian Institute for Research on Public Policy. The late Senator Maurice Lamontagne was a former Minister in the Pearson government. I quote:
The medium-term government strategy was not clear-cut. A few specific fiscal incentives and a less effective tax cut applied to manufacturing but in 1974, a substantial increase in taxes on profits was implemented. More important, after the Canadian dollar was allowed to float in 1970, the rapid rise in the exchange rate significantly dampened the cyclical expansion in business investment by shrinking the market outlets available to Canadian industry.
The coupling of structural and supply-push unemployment and inflation became the dominant phenomenon of this period.
Errors in forecasting and in economic policy made by the government did not help to attenuate these undesirable trends and to achieve greater stability.
Government short-term fiscal strategies were seriously mistaken throughout the period.
However, the seeds of a serious disequilibrium in the government budgetary position had been planted. The government had practically lost control over its budgetary position.
Borrowing Authority
Since 1967, the Liberal governments have spoken about their concern for the deficit and preached the message of restraint. In December of 1967, the then Prime Minister Lester Pearson told Canadians that the government was doing something about the deficit. He said:
By cutting our expenses, and increasing our revenues, as a result, the next budget will be a balanced one.
That year the government spent $11 billion, and there was a net debt of $ 18 billion.
Two years later in August, 1969, Pierre Trudeau told Canadians that:
We'd be on the road to financial disaster if nothing is done to bring spending under control.
Spending was $13 billion and the net debt came to $18 billion. Four years later, the present Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) told Canadians, in his November, 1974 Budget, that:
We must do all we can in these circumstances to restrain the growth of government expenditures.
Spending was $30 billion and the net debt jumped to $24 billion.
Let us move another four years down the road to the next Liberal Finance Minister and his November 1978 Budget, who said:
There can be no weakening in our determination to keep expenditures under tight control.
Spending was $46 billion. The net debt up to $60 billion. Four years later in his June, 1982 Budget Allan MacEachen told the Canadian people that some say the Government:
-should print more money. Others say it should let the deficit rip. But that would fail miserably. Inflation and unemployment would get worse. Interest rates would rise even more. Canada would price itself out of world markets. Recovery would be postponed.
That year, spending was $80 billion and the net debt had climbed to $124 billion.
This last summer the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition told Canadians that:
There are programs that are duplications; there are programs that are wasteful; there are programs that are no longer useful; there are programs that no longer serve a purpose; and I am going to cut that down-
This is the legacy left the Canadian people, left to this Conservative Government. After taking into account the expenditure reductions outlined in this November's economic statement, the Government will spend $100 billion this year, with a net debt by the end of the fiscal year of $191 billion.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, that you look at this record of prudence and sound fiscal judgment espoused by the Liberal government: from spending of $11 billion and a total debt of $18 billion in 1967 to the $100 billion spent this year, and the $191 billion that is net debt. This is the legacy left the Canadian people and this Conservative Government following two decades of Liberal control.
I spend a great deal of time in my riding. I feel that the duty of a Member of this Parliament is to be accessible to the people who put us here. I see a multitude of constituents

weekly and 90 per cent of them ask: "What can we do with the economy the way it is today?" They are not condemning anyone now in power; they are simply wondering what direction we must take to find the light at the end of the tunnel. They are not looking for the quick fix because they know only too well that those who say there is a fast and easy way out do not have a clue as to what they are talking about. They do not wonder how this came to pass. They see the evidence daily in the newspapers, such as, for example, today's edition of The Globe and Mail with its reference to the "Axworthy Empire". People are well aware of the fact that there has been mismanagement and wanton spending in the past that cannot and will not be repeated during this thirty-third Parliament.
Let me close, Mr. Speaker, with another quotation from the Right Hon. Leader of the Loyal Opposition. It reads:
I start from the proposition that there are many things that only government can do. And the first priority is to get these right: fiscal policy, tax policy, trade policy, monetary policy. Then the government must provide a safety net for those who are unemployed, ill, aged, disadvantaged-
The last governments have failed miserably to reach even their first priority, and have worsened the situation for all those mentioned in their second.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I feel I am representative of all Conservatives sitting here today in saying we do not like the prospect of increased borrowing but recognize the necessity of such a move at this time. We as a Government have made a commitment to the Canadian people to bring their financial house back to order. By real restraint and judicious handling of the national purse strings we will realize this goal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment and conclude with a question on the speech made by the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) relating to the need to borrow money. We have had a lesson in history, or at least a scanning of the record of the past. The record was provided to us in a descriptive way. There was not much analysis. My question for the Hon. Member will deal with his analysis.
As he did this historical scanning, I was reminded of another time some 100 or more years ago when the Liberal and Conservative Parties of the day were, by circumstances, being pressed toward a common position. After the Conservative government under Sir John A. Macdonald brought in a national policy, the Liberals resisted it at the time. The Conservatives established a 20 per cent tariff, and the Liberals had a 17.5 per cent tariff. As O. D. Skelton writing about this just before the Great War observed, the difference between protection and free trade became the difference between 20 per cent and 17.5 per cent; 2.5 per cent was sufficient.
I was struck by the fact that the Hon. Member said that a profligate government which squandered money and so on was defeated. Presumably a 4 per cent reduction in expenditure gives us a government which is responsible and prudent. If we
look at the areas in which the trimming takes place, it is startling that they are the environment and others where Canadians lose important services and where there is not a great deal of fat to be wrung out.
In our day what we have in the Liberal and Conservative Parties, for all the rhetoric, is similar policies of restraint which the Liberals, as the Hon. Member documented very well, had been trying to follow. The result had not been economic success, so his constituents-and he does not want to take their comments against himself and his Government-are very anxious. In that continuity of policy we have the grave concern which I expressed that a year hence the request will be for even more borrowing authority.
In all this description of how it has become worse, what actually is wrong with the Canadian economy? What will the Government do other than give us 4 per cent less as a measure of responsibility and urge us all to tighten our belts? As I said before, Canadians have various needs which are not being met. 1 do not want to say yet that the Government will not do anything about it. Important programs are clearly under the knife. Time will tell whether the Government gives a damn about them. Would the Hon. Member tell us what will really be changed other than this minor 4 per cent change?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the Hon. Member's question. We cannot disregard the kind of overspending of which we have seen examples. There were clear indications that many corners had to be cleaned out and that probably many programs needed to be examined by the past government. Many aspiring leadership candidates espoused that. Certainly it was a clear indication to this Government that we should look into the matter. There was another example in today's newspaper. Of course, one of our Cabinet Ministers mentioned that many other Departments had overspent. I do not think the situation is any different from that of a household or a business.
Canadians were looking for some clear signals. I think the Canadian public is already reacting to the indications of the Government by being prudent and by looking at cutting, not at spending. We cannot continue spending more than we take in. Perhaps the Hon. Member can do it, but in the long run I personally think he will run into problems, just as governments will run into problems. I think a very clear signal has gone out to the people of Canada, and they appear to be responding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak against this borrowing Bill and in support of the amendment moved by my colleague. It is the same amendment that was moved by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) when he was Leader of the Opposition. In the very same words, our amendment states:
"that this House holds the opinion that the granting of an authority for the borrowing of a sum greater than the amount which is required to meet the government's needs to the end of the current fiscal year is objectionable in principle-
The Right Hon. Member does not say that it is the government that is objectionable. He says the borrowing is objectionable in principle. This is what we say. It continues:
-and this House therefore declines to give second reading to Bill C-l 1, an Act to provide borrowing authority".
The Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James), in answer to our questions about the principle, repeatedly said, in effect, "Trust me. Trust my Leader. What is wrong for the Liberals to do is right for the Conservatives because the Conservatives have good intentions". He implies that the Liberals had bad intentions, the Conservatives have good intentions. The principles of both the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) disappeared on election day.
What was a matter of principle before September 4 is no longer a matter of principle for the members of the Conservative Party. They are willing to do anything to advance purposes which they claim are good. Unfortunately, they do not tell us in any clear way what those purposes are that are worth $16 billion. They tell us they will create more jobs. All they have done is to lay off people. They tell us they are going to reform the tax system. All they have done is to make the tax

December 4, 1984

system worse by loading more taxes this fall on to low and middle income people without touching with one finger the loopholes that are making the rich richer and the poor poorer. They have not told us one word about what they will do with the money to be borrowed for fiscal 1985-86. They refuse to tell us what they want to do with $16 billion in a fiscal year that has not yet started.
We agree with the principle they expressed a couple of years ago. We regret that they have sold their principle down the river. They sold it for a piece of opportunism in the conduct of the government which the people entrusted to them. Perhaps the people believed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs held those principles. They now find they held those principles only until election day and they are now expended.
What is at stake here is a different principle entirely. What is being operated on is a different principle, the principle of making the rich richer and the poor poorer. This Bill adds $23 billion to the debt. That debt has to be paid by working people and small business people.
The Eton. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) said nobody likes to be a borrower or a lender. He is half right, nobody likes to be a borrower. There are people who just love to be lenders. They become rich. They become billionaires because they are in a position to lend and to charge any interest rate they can force out of the borrowers. The members of the Conservative Party are in league with those lenders. It is the pleasure of the lenders and of this Government to lay still further debts on the people of Canada, for the most part without telling them what they are going to do with the money.
We do not object to the money they are asking for in order to finish fiscal year 1984-85 or even the $2 billion they want because they are not sure they can count correctly and do not know how much money they will have to pay public servants. They are not sure how much they can chop off public servants' wages or other budgets they administer, so they want $5.3 billion plus an extra $2 billion.
We are not arguing with that. We want to focus on the main point. They ask for $16 billion for the coming year without one word of explanation as to what they will do with it. If that passes, and they have a majority, they can do anything they please. This Parliament will not be able to hold them accountable in any effective way.
This flies directly in the face of the teaching given to this country approximately two years ago by the Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church when they put forward two basic principles of Christian teaching that ought to be taken into very serious consideration by the Government of this country and by Members of Parliament. One of their principles was what they called the preferential option for the poor. They warned that if we feed the rich first, the poor get left out and the country is in trouble, whereas if we make sure that the poor get fed, the rich get fed as well. This wisdom has been brought forward for centuries. It is urged upon us not only by
the Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church but by other Christians and leaders of other religions as well.
Their second principle is the priority of labour over capital. That does not mean a choice as between the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. It means a much more basic principle, namely that the work we do today, our live labour, whatever kind of labour we do, must make use of the work we did yesterday or a century ago, which is dead labour, the capital, the tools that we have created in the past which we can use in the present. Our present work must dominate the use of those tools. Those tools must not dominate our present work.
This borrowing Bill enslaves us to the past. It makes the poor poorer in order to make the rich richer. I want to give a few illustrations. Contrary to the Prime Minister's promise to make the tax system fairer, which he has the opportunity to do this month but refuses to do, he promises it will happen some time in the new year, in the sweet bye and bye. What he has done and is doing now is primarily to tax low income people. There is a sales tax which he and his colleagues ridiculed and abhorred when in Opposition. They then changed their principle, turning it upside down on election day. A billion dollars or more a year is to be taken primarily from the pockets of those who can least afford it. Cuts were announced at the beginning of November, $48 million out of a social program which was already nowhere near meeting the needs of the country either for housing or for useful employment. People have been cut from the unemployment insurance rolls by doing what was advocated not only by the former Liberal government but by the Conservative Opposition. People who have taken early retirement, people who have built up pensions and people who have negotiated severance pay are now to lose out on their unemployment insurance benefits because of this Government. To make sure that these people lose out, the Government is hiring 700 snoopers. The Government is taking several hundred people away from the business of counselling workers who are looking for new jobs and has put them into the business of harassing workers to find excuses to cancel their unemployment insurance benefits.
The same Government, without any legal authorization from Parliament, has publicly offered to provide publicly-funded services from the National Revenue Department to help businesses find still more loopholes in the tax structure so that they can pay still less tax. The amount of corporate tax paid has declined sharply in the last several years as personal income tax has risen. The Government will make the amount of corporate tax paid decline still further.

speechtext:
Where did I get that idea? I got that idea from the admissions made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) in answer to a question put by the Opposition. He said, in a statement made in the City of Toronto, that the tax officials will now freely, at public expense and not at
December 4, 1984

cocktail parties after work, tell corporations upon request how they can avoid taxation.
In the last seven years, according to the Economic Council of Canada, there has been $100 billion worth of tax expenditures and forgone revenues under the previous government. This Government is continuing that policy and intensifying it. If that $100 billion had been collected, our deficit would be insignificant. The deficit about which the last government howled and about which the present Government howls would vanish if those revenues had been collected. They should have been collected primarily from the big corporations and the high-income individuals of the country.
In order to try to persuade the public to forget the promises made by the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister has taken on the mantle and stepped into the shoes of the previous Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. The new "Mr. Trudeau" who now sits across from us on the right-hand side of the Chair now says that the deficit is the only problem. He says: "Pay off the deficit at the expense of low-income people and the country will prosper". Those are the same words we heard from his predecessor. The promise is no longer "jobs, jobs, jobs", a promise upon which the Prime Minister was elected. The promise now is "soak the poor".
Seen as a percentage of the Gross National Product, the deficit ought not to be used as the fabricated bogyman that Hon. Members opposite like to use. As a percentage of the Gross National Product, the deficit is smaller than it was during some of the years when Canada thrived after World War II. The deficit is simply being used to cover the rip-off of working people, small business people and farmers.
This is not the change Canadians voted for but is more of the same. The only thing that has changed is that the Conservatives now sit on the right-hand side of the Chair rather than the left-hand side of the Chair. There has been no other basic change of direction. Beyond that, the Conservative Government has intensified the very faults it liked to criticize when it was in Opposition, as shown by the complete sell-out of principle as I have described it in the motion for amendment that is before us.
We have a long history of this kind of policy. The Canadian people have suffered for a long time. This suffering in the main part goes back at least nine years and in some parts even a little further. The erosion of unemployment insurance benefits by policy occurred for several years under the previous government and is continued by this Government. The erosion in the support of post-secondary education occurred under the previous government and will clearly remain no better and perhaps even worse under this Government. The erosion of social housing occurred under the previous government and a further $9.6 million has been cut by this Government.
The erosion of the public health system occurred under the previous Liberal government in connivance with the Conservative governments of many provinces of Canada. We have every reason to believe that that erosion is to continue because we cannot get straight answers from the Prime Minister and his colleagues on the question of universality. One day they are for
Borrowing Authority
it, another day they are against it. They say that they are for it except for certain things. They want to find some ingenious system for preventing a banker who earns $.5 million a year from collecting old age pension benefits. They want people to forget that we have a system for doing that, and that is, the income tax system. This could be done if the present Government were willing to live up to the promises it made last summer.
There is the further erosion of the living standards of working people, small business people and farmers, which has occurred because of the interest system. In the last 15 years, interest payments as a share of the Gross Domestic Product have more than doubled. During the same 15 years, 1966 to 1981, wages as a share of the Gross Domestic Product grew by only 14 per cent. However, the share of interest payments grew by 140 per cent, which is 10 times as much as the share of wages grew. Nothing is being done by this Government to control interest rates just as nothing was done by the last government to control interest rates.
The tools for controlling interest rates are at hand. At one time, those tools were used. Some of us who have grey hair can remember the days when mortgages had, by law, a 6 per cent ceiling. That happened in years when Canada was very prosperous. It can happen again and it would make Canada more prosperous. The lenders who love to lend money at extortionate rates might not be prosperous, but they form a tiny minority of parasites that we do not need to serve as the Government serves them now.
As I said, the main fault with the Bill that we are opposing is that it requests to borrow for the year 1985-86 without proper authority. It is flying in the face of the principle and tradition of Parliament that the Party opposite claimed two years ago and until September 4 to support. No private borrower would be able to get away with something like that. If one were to go to a bank manager and say: "Lend me some money. I will not tell you what I will do with it, just trust me", the bank manager would laugh. The friends of the bankers who sit opposite expect us to take them seriously and to tell our constituents that these are honourable gentlemen who will use the money honestly. They have not given us one reason to believe that they will use the money honestly.
The Government is doing the same thing as R. B. Bennett did when he turned the five-year depression into a 10-year depression using the same policies that the Government is using now. He soaked the poor, increased interest payments, increased the taxes on the poor and made sure that the investors got the gravy. That is how R. B. Bennett undertook to save Canada in the years 1930 to 1935. It took another five years for Canada to find its way out of the hole into which he put the country. I hope the Government will be warned by the example of R. B. Bennett. If not, I hope the people of Canada will take the Government in hand to make sure it does not lead us into 10 years of misery.

Mr. Speaker, the Government talks of creating an atmosphere of confidence in which business can operate. This atmosphere of confidence, Mr. Speaker, which it plans to generate in the private sector will, we are told, solve the country's problems. The Government will not create any private sector confidence with Bills like the one we are debating here. No business would even think of going to the bank and asking for a major loan without telling the bank what it is for. Yet this is just what the Conservatives would have us do. Despite all their rhetoric on fiscal responsibility, they want to borrow $16 billion for the next fiscal year. If the Government is trying to create a credible image for the private sector to see, it should avoid doing what it is doing now. It is behaving in a financially irresponsible manner.
This loan which the Government is asking for is irresponsible. If some businessman in my constituency dared to ask his bank manager for a substantial loan without explaining what the money was for and without demonstrating how the debt would be financed, the bank manager would throw him out. I am warning the Government that it is making a mistake in trying to pursue this dangerous course of action.
I know that a small business could not borrow in the foolish way the Government is proposing. How can the Government create anything but distrust and lack of confidence in that most crucial and vital sector of our economy, small business, if it behaves in the kind of irresponsible fashion which no small-businessman would even consider?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would have us borrow $16 billion without any indication of how the debt will be financed. What good manager would go to the bank for a loan without knowing what revenues would finance the carrying charges? This, Mr. Speaker, is what the Conservatives are trying to do. They are trying hard to manage the flow of information. But if the Minister of Finance himself does not know how he is going to finance the loan, then he is no better at managing borrowing authority than he was at managing information flow in the hotel lobby in Winnipeg.

Mr. Speaker, if the Government wants the permission of the Elouse to borrow $16 billion for the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1986, let it first bring down its Budget, and then we can consider a request for borrowing authority.
Does the Government have any respect for the democratically elected representatives of Canadians? Does the Government have any respect for Parliament?

Mr. Speaker, that is the least we should expect of a Government that claims to be open. Actually, they are more pretentious than they are open, because only yesterday, in the House, Government Members ... In fact, the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), in quoting from the December 1, 1984 edition of The Globe and Mail, claimed that the economic situation had picked up during the third quarter of the year, unfortunately leaving out the next paragraph:

While the federal agency said this growth took place mainly in July, when the Liberals were in power-

Right after that, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez) asked me to tell the House which jobs were lost.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Hon. Member for Chateauguay to read the "Expenditure and Program Review", tabled in the House on November 8 of this year by the Hon. President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret).

Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) knows the exact answer, Mr. Speaker, because he has the projections, but he has refused to table them in the House.

speechtext:
Two years later what do we have? We have Mr. Trudeau reincarnated. We have a new Prime Minister who is doing exactly the same thing. No wonder the people of this country are so cynical about the political process. The Party in Opposition says one thing, it goes to the people of the country and says one thing, and then when it comes into government it does exactly the opposite. The Government is doing exactly what it promised it would not do and what it criticized the Liberal Party for doing two years ago. I do not think that is very principled at all.
Borrowing Authority
The Government is borrowing $7.3 billion for this fiscal year. I can accept that. But it is also trying to borrow $16 billion for fiscal year 1985-86, and I cannot accept that. I have not seen a budget, and I have not seen any precedent for this except for one two years ago in 1982. At that time we had the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition which said that this House holds the opinion that the granting of an authority for borrowing a sum of money other than the amount required to meet the Government's needs to the end of the current fiscal year is objectionable in principle. Those were the words of the Leader of the Opposition. If it was objectionable in principle in
1982,	the same in 1983, then is it wrong in December, 1984? To me a principle is a principle, and if it is wrong in 1982 or
1983,	then surely to goodness it is wrong on December 4, 1984.
I really wonder what the Tories are doing in this House in
trampling on our rights as parliamentarians. If the former Member for Prince Albert, John Diefenbaker, were here, I am sure he would be scandalized but what he sees in this House today. A lack of accountability by the Government which wants a blank cheque. There are a lot of poor farmers in my riding and they cannot go to the Farm Credit Corporation and ask for a blank cheque for the next 10 years. They cannot do that. They have a tough enough time getting money for their farm operations if they present a detailed and well thought out plan to the FCC, let alone ask for thousands of dollars to do something in the future even though they are not sure what it will be. Yet that is what the Government of Canada is asking for. I think that is trampling on the rights of Parliament. Parliamentarians should have a right to say whether or not a certain program is good or bad and should be funded.
The purpose for which we were elected is to decide how to spend the taxpayers' money. But what I see happening across the way with this new Government really makes me very angry and I do not intend to sit silently by and let it borrow all kinds of money for goodness knows what in 1985-86. I wish some of those Members, like the Hon. Member for Mississauga South who was so angry two years ago, would rise up on their hind legs and express some of the same outrage and anger he expressed when he sat here in the House just a few short months ago. If he did that, then I would know he was a very principled man and has the courage of his convictions. He would get up there and fight. I know all kinds of other Members-

I see the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) in the House. I remember very well that, two or three years ago, he often criticized the Trudeau government.

Borrowing Authority
we must change the situation for our people! But now, after September 4, they are behaving just like Mr. Trudeau used to do. This government is not being altogether honest with the people of Canada.

I wish some of these people across the way who got up and showed outrage a few years ago would get up now and say the same thing to the new Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). If they do not do it now, that Prime Minister is going to create an empire in the PMO and the PCO. He will create an empire that makes the empire of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) look pretty small in comparison. The only way for them to stop is for them to get up in this House and put a stop to it. They have the majority of Members.
I wonder what they are going to use this money for, Mr. Speaker. I have had the opportunity to watch first-hand a Conservative Government in my province for the last few years. As I said earlier in the House today, when it took office in April of 1982 there was a surplus in the Saskatchewan treasury of over $100 million. After two years there is a deficit of over $800,000 because of the incompetence of that particular government. The unemployment rate has gone up from 4 per cent to 8 per cent, which is one of the most rapid increases in any part of Canada. The number of people on welfare in my province has gone up by 73 per cent in the last two and a half years.
The Government across the way is borrowing money for the same kinds of programs and purposes as the Government of Saskatchewan and the Government of British Columbia did. They say that confidence, the private sector, and business will do it. Grant Devine says the same thing in Saskatchewan. He says they are open for business and will allow the private sector to do it. They will create all kinds of jobs. Exactly the opposite has happened, Mr. Speaker, and that is another reason why the House should say no to allowing the Government across the way to borrow some $23.3 billion, which is going to put debt upon debt upon the people of Canada in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, this being my first speech in the House of Commons, I would like to start by thanking my constituents in the riding of Duvernay for sending me to Ottawa to represent them. I promise to do everything in my power to honour the trust they have placed in
me. I also wish to say a word of thanks to my colleagues in the House, who were most generous with their help and advice from the first day I started my new life as a Parliamentarian.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Duvernay is the eastern part of the City of Laval and today encompasses an area with a population of over 108,000. Duvernay has a large francophone majority, 89 per cent, while 7 per cent of the population are English-speaking and 4 per cent represent the various ethnic communities. The riding is a veritable paradise for people who like peace and quiet. As far as the economy is concerned, there is a good business environment with the following main industries: manufacturing, construction and the petro-chemical sector. I may add for the information of the House that today, five correctional centres are located in the riding, and even more important, there is a training centre for correctional centre staff, the only francophone centre in Canada.
As a new Member of Parliament I would like to take advantage of the occasion of my maiden speech in the House to say that I fully realize I have yet a great deal to learn, while sharing with my colleagues the business of Parliament and the responsibilities we have to the people we represent here in Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, as a newcomer to Parliament, I have not only a great deal to learn, but also much to offer in the way of experience and my perception of the economic problems facing this country today. Speaking with the people of Duvernay who have entrusted me with the difficult task of speaking for my constituents and explaining their needs before this national forum, I have a deep sense of my responsibility in meeting their expectations and helping them to put the economy of our country back on the right course.
One could compare Canada's distressing economic situation to what happens when we want to renovate an old house. Before you can renovate or expand, you first have to remove any rot from the beams and reinforce the frame. Our Government has made a firm resolve not to act hastily, to ensure that both the economy and the Government will be operating effectively in the interests of all Canadians. I am therefore very happy to be part of a team that is determined to bring this country's horrific deficit under control.
1 would like to add, as the only Italian Member of the Government, that I am proud to represent in this House both the riding of Duvernay and the entire Italian community. Even as a junior Member of Parliament who may not have a great deal of impact on Government decision-making, I am confident, after many conversations with my colleagues, that I will be able to explain satisfactorily the problems of my riding and to act as my constituents' spokesman in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, today is the first time I have spoken to Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority. I am pleased with this opportunity to say a few words about the reasons for tabling this Bill. I would like to mention briefly some of the premises that form the basis for my comments today. I would
December 4, 1984

like to speak to the Bill presented by my colleague, the Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), in my capacity of entrepreneur representing small- and mediumsized businesses.
It is actually somewhat against our principles to support the Bill before the House, because in our opinion, there is a crucial and almost direct link between reducing the deficit and sound management of the Canadian economy in general. However, considering our goal of economic renewal, I wish to express my support for this Bill. No obstacle is as impressive, almost insurmountable and threatening as this federal deficit!
The Bill before the House is aimed at giving the Government an additional borrowing authority of $7.3 billion for fiscal 1984-85, of which $2 billion may be carried forward to fiscal 1985-86. The reserve of $2 billion is intended to cover unpredictable changes in financial requirements. But why has the national deficit suddenly become an important priority on the list of our national policies? After all, we all know that a deficit for a given year is not necessarily a major problem.
However, Canadians are beginning to understand that in recent years, the previous Government registered deficits in years of growth as well as during recession periods. The accumulated deficits have, over the years, generated a cumulative debt of alarming proportions.
This year, the public debt will reach $190 billion, which works out to the equivalent of an individual debt of $24,000 for each Canadian family. Because of this disastrous economic liability we inherited from the previous Government, today we must put the national economy back on course by restoring the confidence of consumers, business and entrepreneurs who are anxious to see a return to responsible management of the country's economy. We do not like borrowing, and as far as that goes, we do not really like the Bill before the House today. However, we are faced with a dilemma. The previous legislation has already given the Government a borrowing authority of $24.5 billion. However, to ensure the proper functioning of our economy, we must go ahead and ask, through Bill C-ll, for a total borrowing authority of $31.85 billion.
A maximum borrowing authority of $16 billion is provided for the 1985-86 fiscal year without possibility of carrying it over to 1986-87, and as the Minister of State has noted, the Bill introduced in this House should enable the Government to meet its borrowing needs until next fall. Later on, a Bill should be introduced after the budget is brought down next spring to cover borrowing needs for the rest of the 1985-86 fiscal year.
Of course, some people might be shocked at the contents of this Bill, but we have no choice: if we had not taken this action, we would very soon have been deeper in debt. To improve borrowing management, to restore a sense of responsibility and active participation in the operation of our
Borrowing Authority
economy and to provide some financial stability, we must support the solution provided by the legislation itself. By its very nature, this Bill constitutes a kind of incentive which will allow us to break the vicious circle of indebtedness; the loss of confidence of consumers and investors has already cost us a lot during the last few years, especially where stable employment is concerned.
The deficit is eroding the very foundation of our economy. It is only by reinforcing the framework of our economy that we can restore business confidence. We need positive investors. We must give them back the motivation to undertake new economic ventures in a true spirit of competition.
Mr. Speaker, the last years of the previous Government are a typical example of a system which I think works like the well-known story about the antelope and the lion. When the lion wants to eat, it runs after the antelope, but when it comes back without having caught the antelope, it does not ask for a grant to tie it down.
I shall close with these words, Mr. Speaker, as the time allotted me has run out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much for giving me this opportunity to say what I think about Bill C-ll to provide borrowing authority, but before I do that, I should like to commend my colleague from Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) for his brilliant statement, particularly since it was his maiden speech.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will not hold it against me if I go into the background of Bill C-ll. Previous speakers have already eloquently said everything that needed to be said, and then some. However, I think it is important, and that is the purpose of my contribution, to emphasize one aspect which is half way between what the Opposition is blaming us for and what we are proposing.
For at least two or two and a half months now, we have been told again and again that Canadians wanted the change of government we had promised during the election campaign. The key word was "jobs, jobs, jobs", and now we are being censured because of the cutbacks. Well, it is true that giving jobs to Canadians will be quite a departure from the former administration, but one thing they seem to forget is that we have promised jobs and, true enough, jobs there will be. But how are we going to do that? Basically, the Opposition is blaming us probably because we are not using the same means they did.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, you will agree that if we were to use the same means, we would obviously reach the same point as the former government-a shameful deficit and an intolerable unemployment rate.
We never said to the people that we had a magic formula, a wonder recipe for creating jobs. We did say quite clearly that we would improve the economic and social climate through a

December 4, 1984
Borrowing Authority
policy of reconciliation and consultation with the various levels of government. And already we have seen tangible results of that consultation and reconciliation process.
Mr. Speaker, this august body stands as evidence of the fact that, not only throughout Canada but especially in Quebec, we have managed to achieve what some people thought was impossible: we were able to have more than 57 Conservative Members elected in the Province of Quebec. Why? Because we consulted one another, each of us in his or her riding, throughout Canada, but particularly in Quebec where I know what is going on, we consulted one another, we all worked together towards a common objective. Many people think that it was a miracle. Well, Mr. Speaker, it was not a miracle, but the result of joint efforts among the various talents we had at our disposal. There you are. That is exactly what we are suggesting to the Canadian people. We want to promote a climate of dialogue with the various levels of government in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite surprised to see once again that the Opposition, particularly the Official Opposition, is raking us over the coals about the cutbacks. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, that was part and parcel of that climate of consultation. We simply had to divorce ourselves from the previous administration, its wasteful ways and its shameless patronage.
As an individual and as a representative of a riding, I am not overly enthusiastic about those cutbacks, particularly when I am directly affected. That is understandable. But when I keep in mind the ultimate objective of this exercise, I am even prepared to vote today on the basic principle of this Bill, since it will eventually help us give Canadians what they expect from us.
As to the other Opposition, the New Democratic Party, they keep on raising objections very forcefully but all in all, they are simply in favour of virtue. I am also in favour of virtue, except that in their case-and I do not know whether they are listening-the problem is that they have no definition of virtue. They always say where they stand once the train has gone by: if it is good, I am all for it, if it is not good, I am against it. But that, always after the fact. Before, we have no idea where they stand. Criticizing seems to be their raison d'etre.
Mr. Speaker, sensible Canadians-they make up the majority in this country-had their say on September 4, and the results are there to see.
