ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING INDIAN SELF-GOVERNMENT Mr. Keith Penner (Cochrane-Superior) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of promoting Indian self-government by:
1.	Announcing support for an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government;
2.	Pursuing actively, a bilateral process of discussion with representatives of first nations on such issues as self-government, natives claims and the elimination of the extinguishment policy; and
3.	Introducing legislation to recognize first nations self-government which should be developed by means of a joint process and utilization of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe that most Canadians would be dismayed and perhaps even outraged if they knew fully that there is a significant group of people in our country calling for emancipation. As difficult as it may be for us to believe, there is a group of people wanting to be decolonized.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) said it very well in committee this morning when he indicated that there is a group of people in Canada who have a sense of powerlessness because they virtually have no control over the most important decisions affecting their daily lives. I am talking about more than a quarter of a million people who are living in Canada and who are weary beyond words of having us standing on their toes. Small nations of people, people who describe themselves as Canada's First Nations, can no longer bear the burden of having us on their backs. The Indian people of Canada want to have their right to self-government, their right to self-determination, recognized in the Constitution of Canada. There is a great need for the federal Government at the next two constitutional conferences between the spring of 1985 and 1987 to be a very strong advocate for Indian people as they seek to have this right defined and entrenched in our Constitution.
I do not think they are asking for too much. For a very long time Indian people have disputed the right of the Government of Canada to run their lives. However, it is only very recently that this situation has begun to receive the public attention it deserves. Their claim to self-government is historically based. Before European settlers arrived on these shores, there were numerous Indian First Nations which were governing themselves quite adequately. They had their own economies, cultures and languages; they traded with one another.
December 4, 1984

The Indian Act of 1876 eroded and undermined these traditional Indian governments in Canada. They were replaced with a form of government which we in our wisdom thought was appropriate for them. We called these new forms of government band councils. These band councils never had any real power. Little chores were delegated to them from time to time, but they never had any real power. All decision-making remained with the government of Canada through the Department of Indian Affairs.
In the mid-1960s it looked as if some enlightenment had arrived in the mind of the government of Canada because it started a new policy called devolution in which it transferred, as was said, responsibilities to Indian communities. Let me examine what that really was. It increased the flow of funds, fairly significantly I should add, and asked band councils to administer certain programs. However, they were never given any decision-making power. They could not participate in the way budgets were derived. They could not participate in the programs developed on their behalf. They were only administrative arms of the government of Canada. I may say that in most cases they administered very well and did so very cheaply on behalf of the government of Canada. All of that has to come to an end because we know how unsuccessful it has been.
Social statistics in Indian communities are a national disgrace. They are appalling, whether we are talking about housing, education, health or any area vital to everyone's daily life. I will not take the time of the House to repeat those statistics. I have done it in the past and they are available. For example, they are available in a public document prepared by the government in 1980 entitled Indian Conditions. So dismal is the record of the government of Canada in directing and controlling the lives of these people that now they are saying, "Give the responsibility back to us; let us manage, control and direct our own affairs; bring to an end this domination and manipulation which has been going on for so many years".
There should not be any misunderstanding in the minds of Members of the House. There is nothing here which is not perfectly legitimate, fair and reasonable. Let it not be thought by any Hon. Member that this is a call for absolute sovereignty or that this is somehow thinly disguised separation. Not at all, not at all.
Indian people are asking to be within the confines and the limits of the Canadian Confederation. Indian people are not asking to be excluded from our Confederation; they are asking to be allowed in. There may be some people in this House and in other parts of the country who will resent these claims for self-determination. This subject is open to misinterpretation, misunderstanding and even ridicule.
Speaking of the relationship between the government of Canada and the Indian people, I should like to quote a statement by Dr. Lloyd Barber of Saskatchewan who once said:
I suppose we tend to react like somebody who has been standing on the other fellow's toes for so long that we are indignant when he wants to pull his foot out.
Indian Self-government
Nearly 100 years ago Leo Tolstoy put it this way:
I sit on a man's back choking him and making him carry me and yet assure myself and others that I am sorry for him and wish to lighten his load by all possible means-except by getting off his back.
Did Hon. Members know, for example, that these artificial governments which we invented and imposed upon Indian people, these chiefs and councils, spend 75 per cent of their time dealing with the administrative overburden imposed upon them by the Department of Indian Affairs? They have been elected in a democratic fashion the same as all Hon. Members of the House were elected. Yet the chiefs and councils have virtually no time to serve the people who elected them and to be accountable to them.
Indian people want the right to govern themselves recognized in the Constitution of Canada. They also want to be recognized by way of statute in this House. They want a self-government Bill that will replace this outmoded and antiquated Indian Act by which we now govern Indian people. Indian government in this country will be distinct. It is not to be confused with provincial governments. It is not municipal government. It is distinct. It is different. It will take many different forms because there is a tremendously rich diversity within the Indian community of Canada. Some forms of government will be tradional, like the potlatch. It is ludicrous to recall a time when the potlatch was actually outlawed. RCMP officers swooped down on a potlatch, arrested people, confiscated relics and objects of art. That is part of our glorious history.
These individual Indian governments will be distinct. Some forms will be suprisingly innovative and modern. I invite Hon. Members to attend on some occasion in the near future an Assembly of the First Nations. It is a parliament like ours. They have a Speaker. Delegates are elected. It is amazing how the order of business is conducted, that with a very large assembly, Members listen to what the others say and try to reach a consensus. When you compare their parliament and ours, what a shame ours is. We appear immature compared to the way their parliament functions.
Whatever form Indian government takes, it must be indigenous government. It cannot be something imposed, such as band government. The powers that these indigenous governments exercise are inherent powers. They belong to them. They are not powers that can be derived from some other level of government whose origins date only to the arrival of Europeans on this shore.
Following recognition by way of the Constitution and by way of statute, which I hope we will pass in this House, there will have to be some protracted and difficult negotiations to define the jurisdiction of these people. The Indian people are quite willing to enter into this bilateral process of government to work out what their jurisdiction will be, but they do not want to proceed by way of consultation.
If Hon. Members have reserves in their constituencies and they visit them from time to time, if I am not being arrogant in

December 4, 1984
Indian Self-government
doing so, may I counsel them to avoid the word "consultation". That word has become so badly tainted in the relationship between the government of Canada and Indian people that it is no longer an acceptable word. In the past, consultation meant a few little discussions after the decision was made. They knew all the time it was a unilateral, imposed decision. They want genuine negotations to determine exactly the jurisdiction that will be exercised by these distinct governments in Canada.
We had such a Bill in the last Parliament, Bill C-52. It was an Indian self-government Bill, but what an inadequate, flawed Bill it was. It was totally unacceptable.
It was a Liberal Bill.

I do not think it was very liberal at all. It was an illiberal Bill. It did the same thing that has been done for so long in the past. That Bill was not developed by way of joint process. It was developed in the usual way, unilaterally, with a few telephone calls and a bit of conversation from time to time. It was not developed bilaterally as the special committee said it should be.
I would like to see that Bill referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but not at second reading stage which would lock us into a clause by clause study. The subject matter could be referred to the standing committee under our new and very able Chairman, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). If we had that Bill in its subject matter form and had the resources to call upon, I believe we could submit for consideration to this House a vastly improved Bill, one that would be acceptable.
I have been talking about legislation. I want to interject very quickly that legislation will not be a substitute for recognition of the right to Indian self-government within the Constitution of Canada. It is merely a step along the way.
Before concluding and allowing other Hon. Members to express their views to the House, my motion also includes reference to the native claims policy. This morning in committee, the Minister indicated that he was going to undertake a full-scale review of that policy. That is long overdue. In reply to a question I put to him in the House today, the Minister stated that part of that review will look very carefully at what is known as the extinguishment requirement.
I wish to take a moment to tell Hon. Members about the extinguishment requirement and see whether they believe that it actually exists. This is how it works. If a native group has a legitimate claim that has been accepted by the government of Canada and enters into negotiations to reach a settlement and a new agreement, at the time that agreement is signed all residual aboriginal rights must be surrendered. The other party to the agreement, the government of Canada, surrenders nothing except what is in the agreement. The other party must surrender everything.
Whoever heard of an agreement like that? Obviously that which is in the agreement must be surrendered. If it is the amount of land or compensation, there has to be a quit claim on that. It cannot be re-opened. To have all other aboriginal
rights surrendered is unreasonable and unacceptable. I believe it is also unconstitutional. Some day that will have to be tested in a court of law.
This policy of extinguishment must go. In his answer today, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development indicated that he is prepared to lead the way in getting rid of it. He will have some problems. He will have problems with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), not because the Minister is an unreasonable man but because this policy somehow got entrenched in the dark corridors of the Department of Justice and it is now believed to be right.
The former Minister of Justice gave me a letter dictated to him by his officials. They were adamant that there could be no movement at all on the extinguishment policy. Today I listened to the Minister of Justice who replied in a confused, halfhearted way. There were more hedges in his answer than in an English country garden.
I conclude by asking whether the Parliament Secretary will give careful consideration to not talking out this motion this afternoon. I ask that he consider having the subject matter of this motion referred to the standing committee. In doing that, there will be no commitment by the Government. Let the standing committee use this motion to do a number of helpful things. This morning in committee, the Minister indicated that he wants to work with the committee, to take it into his confidence. He does not want to use us in some manipulative way. He wants us to be part of the process in developing an Indian policy of which the country can be proud. Here is an opportunity for the Parliamentary Secretary to have a few of his Members make some comments, and before six o'clock agree that the motion not be talked out but be referred to the committee. Other Members will then have an opportunity to express their views in committee and we can carry on for some period of time by looking at these very important, sensitive and difficult issues.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with intent interest to the speech delivered by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). Many of us know the Hon. Member. Those of us who have been Members of previous Parliaments and have worked with him on Indian affairs and on the special task force on Indian self-government know that he has earned a reputation which is perhaps second to none for his regard for the Indian people and for the justice he wishes for them. I commend the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior for the general thrust of his motion.
The report of the Special Parliamentary Committee on Indian Self-Government, which was tabled in the House a little over a year ago, has come to be known as the Penner report after the Hon. Member who just spoke. He and all members of this special parliamentary committee are to be commended for the manner in which they approached the
December 4, 1984

committee's mandate and for the provoking, detailed report which they produced.
In attempting to ensure that Canada's relationship to the Indian First Nations is one of honour and decency, the Hon. Member and his committee have done a great service to all Canadians. By recommending a new relationship which combines historic precedents with current realities, the special committee has set forth a vision for a future in which other governments in Canada might relate to Indian First Nation governments in a spirit of mutual accommodation.
The relationship between the Indian First Nations and the Canadian government is indeed unsatisfactory. Far-reaching change is needed. I think we all agree that an entirely new relationship must somehow be established. It seems to be obvious and indeed reasonable that the people of Indian First Nations must be able to control their own affairs in a manner which respects their diversity, rights and traditions.
We on this side of the House support the concept of a new relationship between the federal government and Indian First Nations. An essential element of the new relationship is the recognition of Indian self-government. This would be beneficial to Canada. The current dependency cycle in which the Indian people and Canada are caught must end. If the communities have the power to determine their own destinies within the Canadian Confederation, they and all of Canada will be strengthened.
The current legal assumptions are not an adequate basis for the new relationship. Now that aboriginal and treaty rights have constitutional protection, Canada requires a new legal framework to ensure that the rights and well-being of the Indian First Nations are protected. Canada must re-order its legal system to accommodate First Nation governments.
Consultations and constitutional discussions have been put under way to determine how self-government can be recognized in Canadian law and how self-government is to be dealt with in the Canadian Constitution. I know the Hon. Member believes that Indian self-government must be specifically stated and entrenched in the Constitution of Canada and that constitutional amendment is the surest way to achieve a permanent and fundamental change in the relationship between Indian First Nations and the federal government. Be that as it may, any such basic change must be carefully considered and accepted by Canadian society at large.
One of the processes through which self-government might be achieved would be bilateral discussions and agreements made within the context of current laws and constitutional arrangements. The multilateral or constitutional amendment process gives provinces an opportunity to co-operate with the federal government in a joint program and policy to advance self-government among Indian peoples in their own communities and on their own lands.
The Royal Proclamation of 1763 which is acknowledged in the Constitution of Canada provided the first basis for recognition of Indian governments and a direct link between First Nations and the Crown. It established a means through which
Indian Self-government
the federal government could enter into treaties and agreements. This arrangement can be used again to enter into agreements with the Indian First Nations so that there will be no confusion with the jurisdiction exercised by the various levels of government.
One thing is obvious to me, Mr. Speaker. The Indian Act is not an acceptable blueprint for self-government. Even if it were to be amended, the Indian Act is not acceptable. Any legislative framework in the area of Indian self-government must be flexible enough to allow for all the governmental arrangements that will be proposed by Indian First Nations.
I am sure a wide variety of Indian governmental styles will emerge, depending upon culture, location, size and the wishes of the people involved. As well, the development of Indian First Nation governments will be sure to proceed at different paces. Needs will change and forms of government will change as well. Such diversity, changes and varying paces are to be welcomed and indeed are to be accommodated.
On an interim basis, pending constitutional change, the federal Government has the option to introduce new legislation which would enhance constitutional entrenchment and which would then reaffirm the special relationship of the federal Government with the First Nations. Through this legislation, the federal Government could then affirm the maximum amount of self-government which it can within its current powers. This possible option is one for which consultations with many sectors are taking place and will continue to take place. The widest possible consultations and participation are necessary if such fundamental legislation is to be developed.
Before colonization, Indian peoples had governments which were accountable to them. This principle has been disrupted by the Indian Act. We support the principle of arrangements which allow Indian people to maintain governments accountable to them. In some instances, joint control will be desirable where First Nation, provincial or federal jurisdictions might overlap. With attitudes of mutual accommodation, sensitivity and respect on the part of provincial and federal governments,
I think agreements on how the jurisdictions could best be jointly exercised would be possible. Such agreements would ensure a workable sharing of power and responsibility.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) is beginning to engage in a serious review in which the Indian First Nations will be involved. This is a review of all existing policies of his Department so that policies may be changed to enhance self-government. He will ensure that only initiatives which lead in the direction of increased self-government are acceptable. This transition process is immediate and will be ongoing. It will be a visible indication of the serious wish of the federal Government to respect a relationship of mutual accommodation.
Recent court decisions have caused a re-examination of federal responsibilities including the degree of obligation of the federal government's specific duty to promote the interests of Indian First Nations. We recognize that there are competing interests. Perhaps there is a specific duty of the Minister to protect the rights of First Nations against encroachment of

December 4, 1984
Indian Self-government
other interests. Perhaps his responsibility must be to act on behalf of the federal Government so that its agreements with the First Nations will be honoured. Ele might be the first recourse of First Nations for action in remedying problems in their relationship with Canada. All of these concepts are now under review by the Minister.
The Government recognizes that there are Indian persons who may not be members of Indian First Nations or who live away from their First Nations lands who continue to have special needs. This is particularly true of those Indian people who live in cities. In this discussion on self-government, I would like to mention that our Government reaffirms its willingness to work with Indian people, Indian First Nations governments, provincial governments and organizations toward arrangements that respect the rights and aspirations of such people so that they may benefit equally with others in the Canadian society in which they live.
The Indian First Nations have shared with Canada the resources of this great and bountiful land. We believe there is a special obligation on the federal Government to ensure that First Nations have the power to plan and implement economic ventures on the community level in whatever forms may seem appropriate to the people of the First Nations. We are moving to adopt those policies and to make them operative. The federal Government will adopt policies which will see that an adequate land and resource base is restored in a manner which does not prejudice the rights and interests of third parties nor the rights of the provinces. Claims for past wrongs must be fairly settled. These are measures the Government is taking so that Indian First Nations will be able to help build the economic bases which are needed if they are to prosper with the rest of Canada.
We note with concern that recent federal initiatives in this regard have been inadequate, as was indicated by the previous speaker. They have been inadequate and inappropriate. They neither serve First Nations nor Canada.
We cannot speak of Indian dependence without noting that Indian First Nations have been denied sufficient resources to maintain themselves for well over a century. As a result, serious deficiencies of community infrastructure exist which we would like to see corrected so that community infrastructure can be improved to a level equal to that of the surrounding communities, but according to priorities, policies and planning established by each Indian First Nation. We will not confuse funding for these purposes with economic development.
What about fiscal arrangements for self-government? We recognize that Indian First Nations require a financial underpinning in a manner which is in harmony with and reinforcing of self-government. The current method of federal funding is totally unsatisfactory and new fiscal arrangements are required. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has recently announced that he is exploring a means of introducing block-funding to Indian governments which are held accountable by their people. Such new funding
arrangements for Indian First Nation governments will enable them to decide how best to meet their people's needs, to set their priorities and to make their own policies. The people of each Indian First Nation will then be able to assume the responsibility of ensuring that these powers are exercised responsibly.
The present duplication, wasteful budgeting and accountability requirements which sap a large percentage of funds allocated by Parliament to benefit the Indian First Nations will no longer be required when ministerial accountability is eliminated in favour of the accountability of Indian governments to their own people. We are exploring a system of direct transfer payments in which Parliament would be asked to take the responsibility for allocation by grants as the means of funding. Eventually, we can see the day when each Indian First Nation will have its own assured sources of income as a result of a control of land and resources, resource revenuesharing, income from investment and economic activity. Until then, interim grants are necessary and justified. We are seeking a way of funding which would allow each First Nation to chose the mechanisms through which it would provide services to its people.
We must find a way, in these times of restraint and fiscal responsibility, to provide a level of funding sufficient so that First Nation governments can provide levels of services on a par with others in Canada, which will allow them to become healthy and productive communities. This can be done only when funds can be expended in accord with their own values and under their own control. This is imperative.
We believe that Indian First Nations which have not yet established sufficient political infrastructure or mechanisms for self-government but which wish to participate in the new arrangements should be able to do so by arranging for a third party to provide services on a contract basis. In some cases these services might come from a provincial government or from the private sector. By moving to these new fiscal arrangements, the federal Government is not only enhancing Indian self-government, but it is reducing unnecessary administrative costs and providing for the best use of scarce funds.
It is a special relationship. The federal Government is moving in these directions not only because it seems to be the right and just thing to do, but because the special relationship between the Crown and the Indian First Nations can best be honoured by enhancing the recognition of Indian First Nations self-government and by providing the resources to make it work. We believe that by moving in these directions the Government will strengthen a relationship with the First Nations which is in compliance with international standards and within the spirit and intent of the original special relationship which was established by our ancestors and the Crown.
In conclusion, there certainly will be areas in which we will be urged to move more rapidly. There can be no doubt about that. There will be those who feel that we are not going far enough. These are uncharted grounds, both for us and for Indian people. There are vast areas which require clarification and others which require fine-tuning. By following the guidelines already set out by the distinguished Hon. Member who
December 4, 1984

presented the motion and the special committee which he chaired, the Government is demonstrating its commitment to the spirit of this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for bringing this motion forward. I think that three parts of the motion are consistent with the report on First Nations self-government which was unanimously approved by Members of all three Parties in the last Parliament.
I was interested in listening to the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), who made a number of suggestions and proposals upon which, he said, the Government would be acting. I simply urge him and his Government to act upon those proposals as soon as possible and to lay them on the table so that the standing committee and the Indian people themselves can examine them and make suggestions and criticims. Then we can get this whole process in place as early as possible. The Hon. Member knows, as we all do, Mr. Speaker, of the urgency of this situation.
There is a general consensus on what needs to be done which is recognized by all people who have looked at this situation. We realize that the present system is not working. It is certainly not working for the Indian people who have been caught in a downward spiral of poverty and dependence. They have been subject to the discrimination and restrictions of the Indian Act. It is not working for the Canadian taxpayer either. We have seen some attempts over the last 110 years to 115 years to force Indian people and Indian communities and governments into a preconceived mould. These attempts have been expensive failures. They have not worked. If they have not completely destroyed the Indian governments which existed prior to the establishment of the Dominion of Canada, they have certainly prevented these Indian governments from functioning in an effective way; they have prevented Indian governments from effectively meeting the needs of their people; and they have prevented Indian governments from helping to keep their people abreast of the needs of the 20th century. They have worked in a very negative manner indeed.
Indian people do not want to become assimilated and have been willing to pay the price of poverty rather than to become assimilated. They do not want to see their nations reduced to the status of municipalities. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, now is the time for action. I was disappointed that there was no reference in the Throne Speech to any action with regard to First Nations government, but I was very pleased to hear what the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary had to say and we hope that the Government will act on those proposals in this section of Parliament.
The previous government acted to the extent of appointing a special committee. After that committee made its report, the government then moved very slowly. Finally, in the dying days of the last Parliament, the government brought in Bill C-52, but it was brought in so late that it was never debated in the
Indian Self-government
House, never referred to committee and, therefore, there was no opportunity for the committee to hear Indian witnesses or make any general examination of any shortcomings or strengths the Bill might have had.
Roberta Jamieson, the liaison member for the Assembly of First Nations, examined the Bill and developed a critique of it.
I would like to quote some of her comments because I believe it is important to have on the record the perspective of one person who was very close to this situation as a member of an Indian First Nation. Miss Jamieson said, and I quote:
C-52 speaks of "special responsibility to Indian peoples", but does not speak of special relationship with Indian governments. The new status for which some bands might be eligible is more corporate than political in nature, and it is acquired from the federal government.
In the Bill, the federal government has been careful to protect its own interests and to protect itself from possible liabilities. In doing so, it has weakened the already weak protection of First Nation interests available under the Indian Act.
There is no recognition of the inherent right of First Nation self-government, nor is there in the Preamble any commitment to seek entrenchment through the constitutional process nor commitment to seek to establish a distinct order of First Nation government. Bill C-52 is not related to nor does it enhance constitutional entrenchment.
Approved bands would have more powers under the legislation than are now available to band councils. But these powers must be exercised within contribution agreements, and the federal government may withdraw its recognition at any time, or be put under a federal administrator, Any law made by an Indian government can be cancelled by the federal government at its discretion.
The federal government maintains total authority over what is acceptable and what is not.
In short, the Bill provides a complex system of cosmetic changes in which the federal government maintains the power and control in the hands of the Minister and the Cabinet.
Bill C-52 continues legislating over Indians and Indian lands. In fact, it seems to ignore the fact that the Canadian Constitution recognizes that aboriginal rights limits Parliament's powers.
No proposal is made for the kind of dramatic change in federal government machinery necessary to allow First Nations to deal with the Canadian government on a government-to-government basis. It does not even establish a new Ministry-everything is left to Indian Affairs. Nor is there any indication Indian Affairs will ever be reduced in size. The new legislation would require increases in the bureaucracy to administer it.
Bill C-52 does not call for revision of the land claims process. No mention is made of accelerated settlement of long-standing grievances, and the concept of "extinguishment" remains as a pillar of federal policy.
No real changes in fiscal arrangements are proposed. Only modifications in current arrangements are suggested. Indian governments will simultaneously have to be accountable to their own people while continuing to be accountable to the Minister for all funds spent and for performance of its governmental functions.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, there are a great many flaws in Bill C-52 and it is not satisfactory. We look forward to something better from the present Government. In that connection, I was pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Erie say that there is going to be the widest possible participation and consultation with Indian leaders. I would urge the Government to bring in funding for the Assembly of First Nations-the funding has expired at the end of the second quarter-so that Indian First Nations can continue with the process of developing their Indian self-government proposals. If there is going to be the widest possible participation, then it is absolutely essential that Indian peoples be funded so that they can participate in a reasonable and responsible manner.

December 4, 1984
Indian self-government
The motion as introduced by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior has three parts. The first part calls for government support for an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government. This coming spring we have another of the constitutional conferences involving the federal and provincial governments. Indian people all across Canada have been very suspicious of the process which involves the provinces. Until now they have only been involved with the federal government. They are suspicious of provincial involvement and have been very disappointed with the results so far. Part of the reason is that the previous government did not take a sufficiently outspoken attitude toward the whole question of the entrenchment of aboriginal rights. The previous government was prepared to sit back until the very last moment when it suddenly decided that it was going to support the concept of aboriginal rights.
What the Indian people, as well as other aboriginal people, would like from the present Government, Mr. Speaker, is that it become an outspoken advocate of aboriginal rights and that it recognize the right to self-government now. There will then be time to mould a consensus involving the Canadian people so that at the time of the constitutional conference the provinces will not be able to say, "Well, we have not had time to consider this. Our people are not prepared", and that sort of thing. We would like to see the Government take an active advocacy role on behalf of First Nation's government.
Second, the motion calls for a bilateral process. There are already many areas where the federal Government and Indian First Nations can negotiate so that Indian First Nations will have much more power under the present system. Certainly the improvements to the land claims process are of the ultimate importance and priority here. Then there is the whole question of introducing legislation, and I urge the Government to do that now.
It is important for all Members of this House and the Canadian people generally to recognize that the situation of aboriginal peoples in Canada is changing. First we had constitutional recognition. Second, we are beginning to get some court decisions which recognize the fundamental nature of aboriginal title. Perhaps the most important of those decisions was handed down in Vancouver just last month. It said that the interest of Indian people in their lands is a pre-existing right, not created by royal proclamation, by Section 18(1) of the Indian Act or by any other executive order or legislative provision. These rights existed before the Royal Proclamation of 1763 which simply recognized those rights. It is important for the Canadian people to begin to recognize the fundamental nature of those rights and to do justice to them. We do not do justice when we continue to insist upon an extinguishment clause, which is really like telling people: I will agree with you that I owe you money if you will agree that I can keep it. That is what we insist on when we demand that Indian people have an extinguishment clause in every kind of land claims agreement that is signed.
There is a general consensus among all people who have looked at this that the present system is not working, that the direction in which Canada and this Government must go is that of the right of aboriginal peoples to govern themselves. Along with that right there must be a granting of the necessary funding so that it is not a meaningless ritual. There must be the provision of an adequate basis, and consensus already exists among people who have looked at this question.
I urge any Members who do not agree with that consensus to study our report. The consensus exists, the time for action is now, and I urge the Government not to talk out this motion but to refer it and its subject matter to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development so that we can continue to make some progress. I underline the need for the Government to continue to make funding available to Indian peoples so that they can make progress on this subject also.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I fully support this motion but because it is getting near six o'clock I will sit down and ask you to put the question.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for bringing forward this motion. He will note that because we debate this issue so little in this House, when a motion comes forward there are many Members who want to participate in the debate. I guess that is a problem we faced during the last number of years. Legislation on this issue has not been forthcoming and, as a result, few Members have an opportunity to discuss the issues in the House of Commons, other than in committee. That is why it has been so important in the past that the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development has taken up the cause of the Indian people in various ways and has been very successful in putting forward ideas and suggestions which may be helpful.
I know that it has been the experience of many of us on that committee over the years that there are many varied and different interests of Indian people across this country and it is very difficult for any Minister or any government to bring forward a piece of legislation which will fit every Indian band or Indian self-governing organization in the country. The desires and aspirations of the Indian people of British Columbia are so different from those of the Indian people of Nova Scotia that when the Bill on self-government was brought forward, immediately Indian nations from across the country had many disagreements with the terms. That is why I am encouraged by the Hon. Member's suggestion that the committee take up the subject matter of this legislation and use it as the basis for our discussions so that the legislation is good for the whole of the nation.
The bilateral process has, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion been essential. I could never understand how we got involved in a constitutional process of attempting to entrench various aspects of the Indian way of life when many of the provinces are not comfortable with the terms that Indian people have
December 4, 1984

using for the last number of years, such as "Indian nation", or with the attempt to eliminate the extinguishment policy. That is why they have been demanding specifics. They do not want problems resulting from entrenchment.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing forward the motion. I hope the committee can take up the work, and I look forward to working with him and other Members as we hopefully continue to foster the work of this Parliament and the Indian people across the country.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) on introducing his motion today. I also congratulate other Members who have worked long and hard over a number of years on this very important report. I had the opportunity a year ago to take part in this committee which travelled to parts of my riding in northern Ontario and to listen to different band members from northwestern Ontario and hear their concerns regarding selfgovernment, dealing with government, and their day-to-day problems.
The Parliamentary Secretary announced today some of the areas which the Government and the Minister are prepared to deal with, such as Indian self-government and the day-to-day problems from coast-to-coast that we have to deal with.

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-ANNOUNCED CLOSING OF STELCO MINE AT RED LAKE, ONT. (B) ASSISTANCE TO MINERS
MINES AND MINING-ANNOUNCED CLOSING OF STELCO MINE AT RED LAKE, ONT. (B) ASSISTANCE TO MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 16 I directed a question to the Hon. Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) concerning the closure of the Griffith Mine located between Ear Falls and Red Lake, Ontario. It was with regard to the 283 jobs, almost one-quarter of the areas workforce, which would be lost should Stelco go through with its intention of closing this mine in April of 1985. I rise today to basically get an update from the Parliamentary Secretary and to offer him an opportunity to read into the record some of the initiatives and moves that his ministry has taken in the meantime.
Adjournment Debate
Specifically, I would like the House to be informed about what discussions have taken place with Stelco and what they have revealed. I am assuming that there has been discussion at the ministerial level with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Sinclair) who was responsible for the ILAP Program, and also with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) who, if the mine in question does close, will be charged with the responsibility of delivering the adjustment programs that will be necessary. I have the assurance of the Minister of State for Mines that the area would qualify for these programs, at least on a "level of assistance similar to that given mines recently closed in Quebec".
In the economic statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that there would be special consideration for single industry towns that were closed down. In his original answer the Minister of State for Mines said that the Government is "ready to assist them to the fullest possible extent with existing programs".
Could the Parliamentary Secretary bring us up to date on discussions with the provincial Ministers concerned, particularly the Ministers of Northern Affairs and of Labour? Have there been any exploratory discussions along the lines of determining a bad ministry and appointing a federal-provincial co-ordinator? Has there been any work done with Stelco in exploring the possibility of obtaining alternative customers? I have in mind the Ipsco plant in Regina, Saskatchewan and the Manitoba rolling mills plant? Would the Parliamentary Secretary take this opportunity to bring us up to date on federal Government initiatives?

speakeroldname: Mr. F. Oberle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-ANNOUNCED CLOSING OF STELCO MINE AT RED LAKE, ONT. (B) ASSISTANCE TO MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to express to the Hon. Member my appreciation for giving us ample notice of his question and for accommodating the Minister in the sense that we are not prepared last week or the week before to respond in greater detail to the question, simply because the Minister was absent from the city.
The Hon. Member is aware of most of the information that I can give him tonight. As he knows, in a press release dated November 15, Stelco announced that the Griffith mine located between Ear Falls and Red Lake, Ontario, would close permanently as of April, 1985. There will be a displacement of up to 282 jobs in that area. Whenever anything like that happens it is very critical and serious. I want to assure the Hon. Member that this announcement arrived here at a vital moment and was taken very seriously.
Yes, there has been dialogue with the company. There have been efforts and examinations into the potential for new customers for the type of product which the mine produces. Unfortunately, it is of a type and a quality that does not lend itself, in present market conditions, to be sold elsewhere.
This mine is the highest cost iron ore mine in Canada, if not one of the highest cost mines in the world. It is a very low

December 4, 1984
Adjournment Debate
volume mine. In other words, there is a lack of economy of scale to consider further operations. It has not been the judgment of any previous government to develop long-term policies with regard to closures of mines. That is the nature of a mining venture. Mining ventures are not only subject to the cyclical nature of that particular industry, but are subject also to the phasing out of an ore body or the volume in the mine.
I can give the Hon. Member the assurance that the Minister has discussed the situation with his counterparts in Cabinet. Every existing program, including enriched ILAP, will be made available to the area. These are training programs, manpower relocation and so on. There have been discussions with provincial counterparts. I cannot tell the Hon. Member which ministry will be the lead agency to service the communities, but everything possible has been done.
In addition to that, the Minister is committed as is the Government to work most expeditiously to develop more longterm policy that would address itself to this general situation; naturally not to this problem because it is an immediate problem and we can only use the existing facilities that we inherited when the Government took office on September 4. There will be very expeditious movement toward a long-term policy that will plan the phasing out of a mine at the inception of a mining venture. That is a critical development involving not only federal and provincial governments and their agencies but industry and unions as well. I want to assure the Hon. Member that everything possible is being done.

subtopic: FINANCE-FUEL SALES TAX REBATE-POSITION OF BULK FUEL DEALERS
FINANCE-FUEL SALES TAX REBATE-POSITION OF BULK FUEL DEALERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker this is further to my question raised November 29 concerning rebate of sales tax on farm fuels. I would direct my remarks to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier). Let me say first that this Government is to be congratulated for moving quickly to fulfil another major promise to provide fuel tax relief to hard-hit primary producers such as farmers, fishermen, miners, and laggers.
I note that Bill C-12, to amend the Excise Tax Act, was read for the first time November 26. Hopefully it will move to second and third reading soon. The amendments will provide for a rebate of sales tax of 3 cents per litre on gas and diesel fuels used in off-highway primary production. As well, the producer will be exempt from the recent 1.8 cent per litre increase in the petroleum compensation charge. Thus the total rebate will be 3 cents plus 1.8 cents, for a total of 4.8 cents per litre or almost 22 cents per gallon, effective December 1, 1984.
Unfortunately there are several problems associated with the rebate. Notwithstanding a communique concerning the program issued yesterday by the Hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty), there appears to be confusion about
application and, even worse, the possibility of discrimination against a large number of bulk fuel dealers.
Since my riding in southwestern Saskatchewan is largely agricultural, I will use the farm community as an example. The sale tax is essentially a refinery tax, and it is payable at the time of sale by the manufacturer. Some bulk fuel dealers- and these are the dealers in villages, towns and cities who retail to the farmer, notably Imperial, Shell, Texaco and Petro-Canada who hold fuel on consignment from headquarters-have an inventory free of sales tax. In effect they are agents of the refinery. They will be in a position to give an immediate sales tax rebate of 22 cents per gallon to their customers.
On the other hand, many bulk fuel dealers have purchased their inventory for resale. I am told that these dealers include Gulf and Husky as well as all co-operatives and independents. These dealers hold inventory on which sales tax has already been paid. Therefore, in order to reimburse themselves they must pass the tax on to the farmer.
1 should like to examine the producer end for a moment. The rules appear to say that the farmer is to secure a bulk fuel permit from Revenue Canada and present it to his dealer. If the dealer has tax free inventory, obviously the rebate benefit of 22 cents per gallon will be given immediately at the time of the sale. However, if the dealer has tax paid inventory, then he must collect the 22 cents from the farmer and tell him to remit an application form along with purchase invoices to Revenue Canada for a rebate.
The average farmer purchases some 10,000 gallons or
45,000	litres per year of farm gas and diesel fuel. The rebate will mean something in the order of $2,200 annually. Let me assure the House that most farmers will be inclined to go for their fuel where they can get it for 22 cents per gallon less up front. They do not want to mess around with the forms and the usual government delays. I see the potential sales of those dealers with tax paid inventory being very seriously affected, through no fault of their own. We realize the difficulties in administration owing to the nature of the tax at the refinery level, and because the rebate is going to only a certain segment of the population. Nevertheless, there appears to be no reason to discriminate against certain dealers.
There appear to be two possible solutions. The first would be to require all dealers to collect the tax. All producers would then submit their invoices and application forms for rebate. Such an application form could be combined with the existing application for the 1.5 cent per litre excise tax refund. Producers could then apply on the same form for all three rebates-the three cents per litre on the sales tax, the 1.8 cent per litre on the petroleum compensation charge and the 1.5 cent per litre excise tax, for a grand total of 6.3 cents per litre, or something in the order of 28 cents per gallon.
The second alternative would be to permit those dealers holding tax paid fuel inventory to give the rebate to their qualified customers over the counter and then seek refund from the Government of the sales tax not collected. If this alternative were selected, the dealers would have to be assured
December 4, 1984

of speedy reimbursement, perhaps through a system of revolving credits.
Another possibility which may occur to the bureaucrats is to resort to coloured fuel to distinguish inventory available to primary producers from that available to the general public. Bulk dealers, who have only so many compartments in their delivery trucks and limited holding space, unanimously beg the Government not to resort to the use of dyes.
In conclusion, I trust the foregoing has explained the potential problem faced by many bulk fuel dealers. The rebates are to take effect from December 1. It is now December 4. Of course the amendments are not yet law; there is still time to rectify the problem. I raise it now in the hope that remedial action can be taken. The producers and dealers need a rebate system that is fair to all and simple to administer.
I again congratulate the Government on instituting a system which will provide much needed relief. At the same time, I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to comment on whether a solution to this apparent problem is at hand.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-FUEL SALES TAX REBATE-POSITION OF BULK FUEL DEALERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on my first appearance on the "late show", I have been asked to talk about rebates, and I will try to do so with all the dignity this requires.
In fact, we are concerned here with a fuel sales tax rebate and the differences existing in the position of bulk fuel dealers.
The Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) has expressed some valid concerns with respect to the fuel sales tax rebate program announced in the Government's economic message on November 8 of this year. He observed, quite rightly, that some dealers have tax-free inventory while others have tax-paid inventory. The former are therefore free to offer a direct rebate, while the second group's customers must apply especially for the rebate.
The simple solution would be to demand that all people benefiting from the rebate submit claims. We realize that this procedure will not be attractive to farmers, who would probably prefer to do without the administrative red-tape. On the other hand, they are familiar with the practice because it has existed for a number of years in connection with the one and a half cent excise tax rebate per litre of gas.
Another more complex solution might be to allow retailers to claim the rebate on behalf of the primary producers in the case of bulk sales. Retailers would then be required to provide names, sales permit numbers, sales volume and proof that the rebate was indeed credited to the client. This solution, however, does pose a few problems.
First of all, it would impose an additional administrative burden which some retailers would certainly not be willing to take on. Second, identifying clearly what constitutes a bulk
Adjournment Debate
sale might also be a major problem. Third, since the claiming party is not the actual recipient of the rebate, there is a risk of a tax "leak"-no pun intended-which might take on increasing proportions. Finally, retailers electing to submit claims on behalf of their customers would have to wait some time before receiving the funds claimed from Revenue Canada.
The Government is now consulting with the fuel sector, and we are confident that a solution satisfactory to all parties concerned will emerge from these consultations, which are being held as part of the regular policy of this Government.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PLIGHT OF NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERMEN NOT ELIGIBLE FOR BENEFITS. (B) LEVEL OF ASSISTANCE FOR AFFECTED CONSTITUENCIES
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PLIGHT OF NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERMEN NOT ELIGIBLE FOR BENEFITS. (B) LEVEL OF ASSISTANCE FOR AFFECTED CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a subject that came up in the House today. As some Members will know, the Minister announced today a $6 million program for fishermen and plant workers who were affected by the inshore fishing season this year. That is welcome news. I congratulate the Minister on it, but I would say to her that it is too late. I wish she had agreed to the request we made some six weeks ago.
1 raised a question in this House, as did my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). We wrote and spoke to the Minister pointing out the seriousness of the situation. We tried to help the Minister to understand, as I am sure the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) did, that fishermen and plant workers have no recourse; there is no safety net, no alternative. If the fish do not come ashore because of ice, dirty water or whatever, there is no recourse. The system is built in such a way that the welfare system will not support them adequately. There is no alternative for fishermen and plant workers caught in that situation.
If one responds at the proper time, such as in October, one can work out projects that will be beneficial to the community. As it now stands, it will take about another week to identify where the fishermen and plant workers are who are affected. We will then have to hastily design projects which will last until the end of March. You can repair some gear and do some inside work, but you cannot build a slipway or repair a wharf in the winter. Nor can you fix a stage. These are things that cannot be done when frost and snow is on the ground. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that most of the fishermen affected here are on the northeast coast of Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador.
I welcome the news, but I say to the Minister that it is too late. In September and October we told her that she should act then. She insisted on waiting for the end of the fishing season. Sure, the fishing season is not legitimately over until Novem-ber-December, but the reality for many communities is that it finishes as of September.

December 4, 1984
Adjournment Debate
I welcome the news but I would urge the Minister to act quickly next year, or the next time this happens. Please God that it will not happen next year. I believe it is an act of God. If it does happen next year I would urge the Minister and the Government to take speedy measures, bearing in mind that we are dealing with disadvantaged people who suffer through no fault of their own, and to whom there is no recourse or alternative. An ex gratia payment is the only alternative. I welcome the Minister's announcement today. I simply wish she had made it six weeks ago.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PLIGHT OF NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERMEN NOT ELIGIBLE FOR BENEFITS. (B) LEVEL OF ASSISTANCE FOR AFFECTED CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
As my colleague pointed out, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has already said that we are monitoring the fishing situation very closely. Fisheries and Oceans Canada have advised us that, according to recent data, roughly 1,100 Newfoundland fishermen might have enough weeks of insurable employment to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits this winter. That figure has been confirmed by the United Fishermen and Food Workers Union.
We have also been advised that most fishermen along the coast of Labrador might be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits and that the situation in the south-east region has improved since Fisheries and Oceans Canada have authorized higher herring quotas.
The special fund mentioned by the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was in fact a subsidy to provide assistance to fishermen in areas where during the normal fishing season, fishing is restricted because of icing conditions. Last spring, the ice remained longer than expected, which left the fishermen in many communities without work and without income, the winter period of unemployment insurance benefits having expired. This special initiative was taken by Employment and Immigration Canada, but the money did not come from the Unemployment Insurance Fund.
The Minister recognizes the importance of short-term job creation programs for people in the fishing industry who are not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. I am therefore happy to inform you that the Minister of Employment and Immigration has allocated another $6 million to the Canada Works Program to provide assistance to fishermen and processing plant workers who are suffering because of the plight of the fishing industry. The Minister has already provided that information to the Hon. Member, in a letter he may not have had the chance to read.
I would also like to inform the House that we are in the process of amending the National Employment Service regulations with respect to the referral of applicants for Canada Works Projects. Such an amendment will ensure throughout Canada that any fisherman or fish processing plant worker who has not qualified for unemployment insurance will be referred as a priority for projects approved under the Program.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress once again that we are closely monitoring and that we will keep monitoring the situation in the fishing industry, and that the Minister has taken firm steps to improve that difficult situation. I can also assure the House that problems related to fisheries will be discussed during the talks to be held with the provinces on the Government's overall directions in the area of job creation and training.
